West Bengal's Criminal Investigation Department (CID) has taken over an investigation into allegations that a man impersonated State Minister Kshudiram Tudu to influence the ongoing Staff Selection Commission (SSC) recruitment process. The accused, identified as Zulfiqar Ali of Deganga, was arrested by Bidhannagar Police following a written complaint submitted at Bidhannagar East Police Station by the SSC Secretary regarding WhatsApp messages allegedly sent to exert influence over the recruitment. CID Director General and IGP Natarajan Ramesh Babu confirmed that further details would be shared as the investigation proceeds.

The text notes this case is separate from an earlier September 15 incident in which Jharkhand's CID arrested two individuals—Sanjeet Kumar of Ranchi, who allegedly operated Shivangan Coaching Centre—for collecting money from candidates by promising to help them clear the 14th Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC) preliminary examination. The source presents these as alleged irregularities without confirming guilt or providing additional evidence beyond the reported arrests and complaints.
items.title: Man Arrested for Allegedly Impersonating Bengal Minister Kshudiram Tudu in SSC Recruitment Case

items.summary: Paolo Bulgari, grandson of Greek silversmith Sotirios Voulgaris and longtime head of the family jewellery business since the mid-1980s, has died in Rome at age 89. His family announced his death on Saturday, describing him as "the greatest jeweller of our time" while praising his humanity and entrepreneurial talent. Born in Rome in 1937, Bulgari joined the company shortly after leaving school to work alongside his father Giorgio, developing expertise in precious stones that shaped his later design and business career. Under his leadership with brothers Nicola and nephew Francesco Trapani, the brand shifted away from delicate Parisian aesthetics toward bold gemstones, rich yellow gold, generous proportions, and distinctive colour drawn from ancient Rome and Italian heritage, while expanding into New York, Paris, Geneva and Monte Carlo and diversifying into watches, perfumes, leather goods and hotels. In 2011 the family sold a controlling stake to French conglomerate LVMH in a deal valued at more than USD 5 billion, ending decades of direct family control. Bulgari also established the Paolo Bulgari Foundation in 2019 with his wife to support schooling and job training for young people in disadvantaged neighbourhoods on Rome's outskirts; he wrote that "at the origin of my surname there is a story of migration." His funeral is scheduled for Monday at the Basilica of Santa Croce in Rome.
items.title: Paolo Bulgari, architect of global luxury empire, dies at 89

items.summary: Xiaomi is selling its electric vehicles outside China for the first time ever, launching this week through local distributor Gargash Prime Automotive rather than operating its own retail network. The company's SU7 sedan, YU7 crossover, and Skynomad SUV are now listed for sale across the United Arab Emirates. Xiaomi CEO Lei Jun confirmed that Western car market entry would be announced at the APEC CEO Summit in Shenzhen on November 17, with official expansion into those markets scheduled for next year (2026). CarNewsChina reports Gargash Prime is offering 13 variants spanning the SU7 sedan, YU7 SUV, and Skynomad extended-range electric SUV lineup. Pricing starts at 169,900 AED (~$46,200) for the SU7 Standard and rises to 375,900 AED (~$102,000) for the range-topping SU7 Ultra. The SU7 Ultra is highlighted as a performance flagship with 1,548 hp from three electric motors, a sub-two-second 0-100 km/h time, and a 217 mph top speed. First customer deliveries of the SU7 Standard and Ultra, YU7 Standard, and Skynomad N70 Pro are scheduled for December (of this year), with remaining variants following in February 2027. The article notes these sales occur amid a broader wave of Chinese-built EVs entering Europe and Canada.
items.title: Xiaomi Begins Overseas EV Sales in UAE, Marking Its First Global Car Launch

items.summary: On Saturday, Bahrain accused Iran of striking a civilian industrial facility on Sitra Island—home to state oil company Bapco's refinery—causing a fire with no reported casualties. The interior ministry confirmed the attack without specifying its location, while residents described smoke rising over the island and Iran's Fars agency attributed strikes against two US bases there (Sheikh Isa and Juffair) to Revolutionary Guards action in response to alleged US actions. Simultaneously, UKMTO reported one tanker struck by an unknown projectile as it transited Hormuz with no casualties, while a second vessel was hit in its engine room; Iran later claimed the ship caught fire after entering a restricted zone and striking a mine—though US Central Command stated last month that mines had been cleared from main routes. These attacks ended a weeks-long lull following late-February US-Israeli strikes on Iran, which began an ongoing conflict over Hormuz, through which one-fifth of global oil flowed before the war; since summer, US forces have escorted ships and helped Gulf states export 1.5 billion barrels while maintaining its own counterblockade of Iranian ports. Diplomatically, deputy foreign minister Kazem Gharibabadi said Iran considers the US economic blockade an act of war it will lift through necessary measures, while Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi called for talks to succeed and a rational lifting of the blockade—though Tehran insists on ending hostilities across all fronts, unfreezing assets, removing oil sanctions, and halting the counterblockade. Separately, Iran reported shooting down a US drone over Qeshm Island after American jets struck an Iranian missile site there Tuesday; President Masoud Pezeshkian warned that strikes on energy infrastructure would worsen winter power shortages, prompting his national electricity company head to announce rolling blackouts from Sunday due to fuel supply constraints. The summary reflects claims attributed to state media and officials without independent verification.
items.title: Bahrain Accuses Iran of Striking Industrial Site and Tankers in Strait of Hormuz

items.summary: The National Centre for Seismology (NCS) reported that a magnitude 4.1 earthquake struck Myanmar in the early hours of Sunday, November 22, 2026. According to an NCS post on X, the quake occurred at 2:35:57 AM Indian Standard Time, with its epicentre located at latitude 24.404 North and longitude 94.616 East in Myanmar, at a depth of 95 kilometres. The NCS provided these details as recorded values rather than an assessment of any impact or damage.
items.title: Myanmar Records 4.1 Magnitude Earthquake

items.summary: On Saturday, Iran launched two waves of drone and ballistic missile attacks on four US bases in Bahrain—home to the Fifth Fleet headquarters—with Fars news agency naming Sheikh Isa and Juffair among them. Iranian Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) claims stated that Patriot batteries and radar were hit, but neither Bahrain nor the US military confirmed these assertions; Bahrain instead reported intercepting several strikes and a civilian fire at an industrial compound with no injuries. Separately, explosions in Sirik, southern Iran, followed earlier US retaliation against Iranian facilities. In the Strait of Hormuz, at least three oil tankers were attacked Saturday: UKMTO said two tankers were struck separately by projectiles while exiting the Persian Gulf, and Iran's navy reported a tanker hit a mine east of the strait and caught fire—no casualties in any case. As these incidents rose over the past week, more than 14 Iranian tankers reportedly gathered off Kharg Island to break what Iran calls an illegal US blockade; deputy foreign minister Kazem Gharibabadi warned that breaching it could trigger a fierce response targeting Gulf energy infrastructure if engaged by the US military. Diplomatic activity continued in parallel: Qatar hosted talks with Iranian officials on Friday evening, and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi suggested reopening the Strait of Hormuz would be feasible if the US ended the blockade and lifted sanctions. President Trump separately said he sought a permanent deal to prevent Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons while ruling out regime change; however, the Institute for the Study of War noted that Iranian attempts to run the blockade create dilemmas for Washington—either collapse the blockade or risk war with unideal political costs—but no concrete outcome was stated.
items.title: Iran Strikes US Bases in Bahrain as Tankers Prepare to Break a Naval Blockade

items.summary: The article examines why people increasingly turn to absurd memes, sarcasm, and dark humour as an escape from stress caused by rising screen time and information overload. It presents six explanations: humour can make overwhelming situations feel less serious; relatable content about anxiety or burnout creates a sense of shared experience; dark humour lets people process difficult emotions through irony rather than direct confrontation; memes provide low-effort, instant entertainment compared to longer videos or articles; self-deprecating jokes reduce pressure around everyday imperfections and help with social fitting-in; and endless scrolling can paradoxically worsen the very screen fatigue it was meant to relieve. These points are attributed to specific sources: psychiatrist Dr Harish Shetty notes that dark humour may help people acknowledge uncomfortable feelings, while Gen Z content creator Amaan links the trend to dopamine-seeking behaviour and self-deprecating jokes as a way to avoid embarrassment. Raahi Doshi, a Gen Z graduate, cautions that using reels purely to suppress emotions can become unhealthy but remains acceptable for casual fun. The piece concludes with the caveat that memes offer only temporary relief rather than genuine rest or solutions, suggesting people should sometimes put their phones down instead of relying on digital content to manage stress.
items.title: Why Absurd Memes And Dark Humour Are Becoming A Popular Coping Mechanism

items.summary: On Saturday, Mexican forces captured Fausto Isidro Meza Flores—known as 'El Chapo Isidro,' one of the FBI's most wanted fugitives—in Guasave, Sinaloa, after an overnight operation left seven alleged cartel gunmen and four Mexican soldiers dead. The firefight erupted around 7 p.m. on Friday when armed forces came under attack with guns and explosives from suspected cartel operatives; authorities then established a security perimeter before entering the building where he was located to detain him. Because of intense resistance—including at least 10 roadblocks with burning vehicles—Mexican army and National Guard special forces could not extract Meza Flores until 4 a.m., after which eight people were detained total, including his No. 2. He was flown to Mexico City to appear before prosecutors. Meza Flores had led the Beltrán Leyva cartel and later headed his own group, the Meza-Flores Transnational Criminal Organization; he was also an ally of 'Los Mayos,' a Sinaloa Cartel faction designated as a foreign terrorist organization by the Trump administration last year. Mexico's government said intelligence from the Trump administration helped authorities capture him but provided few details on how coordination occurred. The U.S. had offered a $5 million reward for information leading to his arrest, and he was wanted for trafficking drugs into the United States and illegally carrying firearms. Following the capture, residents of Guasave—part of a 290,000-person municipality—reported widespread gunfire, burning cars and businesses, circling helicopters firing on people below, and thousands taking shelter in grocery stores; burned-out trucks blocked roadways leading into town. Mexican Security Secretary Omar García Harfuch posted that armed forces would remain deployed to protect civilians while lamenting the four soldiers killed. The DEA commended Mexican authorities as a security win, and U.S. Ambassador Ronald Johnson said such results 'don't happen overnight' but are built on cooperation between partners. The capture is part of President Claudia Sheinbaum's more aggressive crackdown on cartels amid pressure from Trump; homicides have reportedly dipped significantly during her two years in office. However, experts warned the arrest could trigger further violence: security analyst David Saucedo said it reflects a longstanding 'kingpin strategy' that captures leaders without dismantling organizations—here, only Meza Flores and his No. 2 were taken while street-level dealers, businesses, and political and police connections reportedly remain intact—and noted such tactics often fuel violent power disputes among warring factions in the region.
items.title: Mexican authorities captured cartel leader 'El Chapo Isidro' in a firefight that killed at least 11 people

items.summary: A recurring workplace anecdote—an anonymous Reddit commenter describing a boss who passively shames an employee for minimal engagement in group chats—raises the question of why Gen Z feels singled out. Career site Forage, written by a Gen Zer, notes that this generation is commonly labeled 'difficult' or 'hard to work with,' and cites a 2023 Resume Builder survey of 1,344 managers and business leaders in which 74% rated Gen Z harder to work with than other generations. However, the text treats this figure as measuring managerial perception rather than actual workplace performance, and flags that the company commissioned it. The Hindu frames generational labels as provisional stereotypes, questioning whether blamed traits are unique to Gen Z or simply reflect what any young generation experiences when taking on responsibility, while noting that older Indians' memories of hardship like ration-shop queues shape their views of work and entitlement. College counselor Kimberly Lobo attributes feeling targeted to overlapping forces—developmental age, greater exposure, social media, comparison, and environmental stress—and argues Gen Z is not simply more sensitive but grows up in a highly exposed, comparative environment while meeting normal developmental needs for identity formation; she rejects the 'fragile' characterization. Joe Moraes, 20, from Mumbai, describes criticism as landing equally online and offline because digital growth has blurred where identity lives, whereas his parents' generation received feedback privately. The text observes that generalization turns one person's thumbs-up into a verdict on all twenty-somethings, and quotes Geeta Giddi, whose 19-year-old son listens but ultimately does as he pleases—illustrating how the same behavior reads as disobedience to one generation and independence to another. The article concludes that feeling targeted may reflect constant observation, comparison, and judgment rather than oversensitivity.
items.title: Gen Z Feels Targeted at Work Despite No Evidence of Worse Performance

items.summary: A Russian ballistic missile struck President Volodymyr Zelensky's hometown in central Ukraine on Saturday, killing two people and wounding dozens. Hours after the attack, Zelensky reaffirmed his country's determination to join NATO.
items.title: Russia launches ballistic missile attack on central Ukraine

items.summary: Mexican special forces captured Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as "Chapo Isidro," during an operation in Sinaloa on Friday night. Footage released by Mexico's Defence Department shows heavily armed soldiers escorting the detainee into an army vehicle. Meza Flores was among the FBI's 10 most-wanted fugitives and is accused of trafficking drugs into the United States and illegally carrying firearms. Mexican authorities stated that intelligence provided by the Trump administration helped lead to his capture, though this claim originates from a source whose reliability should be independently verified rather than accepted at face value. Following the operation, violence erupted in the region, prompting security forces to remain deployed to protect civilians.
items.title: Mexico Captures FBI Most-Wanted Cartel Figure 'Chapo Isidro'

items.summary: A Russian cargo ship caught fire after being struck by drones on Saturday and subsequently drifted into Finnish waters, according to reporting from Kyiv. The vessel is affiliated with a major Russian military logistics company. Analysts cite a clear motive for the targeting; however, Ukrainian authorities have not confirmed or denied responsibility for the attack.
items.title: Russian Cargo Ship Set Ablaze by Drone Attack in Gulf of Finland

items.summary: Cameroon's under-17 team opened their FIFA U17 World Cup campaign in Doha with a 2-1 defeat to Venezuela, ending the match without securing its first points. Coach Thomas Libiih attributed the loss partly to lost momentum, stating that Cameroon missed some rhythm and did not deserve the result but slipped into it. Midfielder William Gueke described the team as slow to start in the first half before improving after halftime, framing the performance as a learning experience while reaffirming their goal of winning the tournament. Captain Krys Karel noted that Cameroon created chances but failed to convert them. The defeat leaves the squad seeking regrouping ahead of its next Group K match and focused on earning points to keep hopes of advancing to the round of 32 alive.
items.title: Cameroon U17s Lose World Cup Opener to Venezuela

items.summary: European Council President Antonio Costa has proposed a revised draft of the 2028 to 2034 EU budget, reducing it by €204 billion from an earlier European Commission proposal that drew criticism—especially from northern members including Germany—for being too large. The revision introduces new revenue channels intended to keep national contributions at a reasonable level; Costa described the plan as realistic and confident it provides a basis for agreement. The centerpiece is a tax on companies with annual digital-activity turnover of at least €50 million in the EU and €750 million worldwide, charging an annual contribution equal to 3% of net turnover from online advertising, digital intermediation services, and user-generated data. Other new own resources include taxes on tobacco products and electronic waste. Divisions persist: France called the draft 'deeply disappointing' and said it does not provide a basis for agreement because it falls short on Common Agricultural Policy income support for farmers.
items.title: European Council President Proposes Smaller EU Budget Funded in Part by a Big-Tech Tax

items.summary: A Russian ballistic missile double-tap strike on Friday evening hit Ukraine's southern city of Kryvyi Rih, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's hometown, killing two people — a 7-year-old boy and a 20-year-old woman — and wounding about 60 others, including several children, according to Ukrainian officials. City administration head Oleksandr Vilkul reported that the strikes caused fires and damage to roughly 25 apartment buildings, a hospital, schools, and an industrial facility via Telegram. Moscow separately confirmed another strike on Friday night in Kryvyi Rih, with Russia's Defense Ministry saying a thermal power plant was hit along with a power substation in Rivne; both facilities supply electricity to industry supporting Ukraine's military. The attacks came amid little progress in talks to end the nearly five-year-old war and after Ukraine struck the Kerch bridge linking Russian-occupied Crimea with Russia three times this week, prompting Putin to vow a "painful" response over what Moscow views as vital supplies for its southern forces. Beyond Kryvyi Rih, Russia reportedly struck a cargo vessel near Odesa carrying dual-use goods; an 11-person drone attack wounded people in Kharkiv including two children and one person was wounded in Kyiv; Ukrainian drones wounded three people in the Bryansk and Belgorod border regions of Russia; and Finland detected a Saturday morning drone attack on a Russian cargo ship in the eastern Baltic Sea, with Prime Minister Petteri Orpo warning that the war is "spilling over into our immediate vicinity." Zelenskyy warned NBC that the damaged Kerch bridge "will not remain standing anyway."
items.title: Russian ballistic missile strikes on Kryvyi Rih kill two and wound dozens

items.summary: Since taking office nearly two years ago, the Trump administration has expanded support for coal through executive orders and federal funding to keep aging plants open beyond their planned retirements. In September 2025, following passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act earlier that year, the Department of the Interior opened 13.1 million acres of federal land for coal leasing during a "Beautiful Clean Coal" event, with Secretary Doug Burgum citing reduced royalty rates and increased available acreage as economic and national security measures. An Environmental Defense Fund analysis of the 184 operating coal plants connected to the grid found that 90 receive financial, regulatory, or operational support from the administration — including $950 million in public funds distributed across 24 plants and Clean Air Act exemptions granted to 70 plants. EDF's Saruri Sarang characterized these measures as "cash handouts, free passes to pollute, and requirements to stay online past their retirement dates," arguing they raise electricity costs while increasing pollution for communities. The EPA's Mercury and Air Toxics Standards had reduced mercury emissions from coal- and oil-fired plants by more than 90 percent by 2026 after taking effect in 2015, with a further update in 2024; however, the administration permitted several firms to request exceptions on the basis of upgrade costs. The average U.S. coal plant is 44 years old and requires upgrades to operate effectively. Carbon emissions from the electric power sector rose 4 percent in 2025 relative to 2024 per the U.S. Energy Information Administration, with coal-fired electricity generation up 13 percent and raising coal-related CO2 emissions by 78 million metric tonnes. The article frames these figures as evidence that continued public financing of aging plants threatens human and environmental health while costing taxpayers billions rather than delivering cheaper power.
items.title: Trump Administration's Coal Support Costs Taxpayers Billions With Little Benefit

items.summary: Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said that, following trade agreements reached between UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham and European leaders in Brussels on Friday, the possibility of the UK rejoining the EU could be examined during informal discussions. The three announced deals covered food and drink standards, emissions trading, and a youth mobility scheme under which 100,000 young Britons would gain access to live, work, study, and travel in the EU with reciprocal rights for Europeans in the UK; Burnham estimated this agreement would add 0.5% to GDP, equivalent to £17bn. Miliband characterized these agreements as the limit achievable before the next general election, while noting that further brainstorming discussions with Brussels were planned over the following year and ahead of a UK-EU summit. However, the deals face potential disruption within six months if the EU blocks them unless European students pay domestic-level fees at British universities—a tuition-fee proposal reportedly not yet agreed—though Miliband insisted the food exports, energy, and youth mobility agreements would proceed regardless. The arrangements are scheduled to enter force in 2028 through legislation introduced next week. Labour has maintained its manifesto red lines since entering government in 2024, ruling out rejoining the single market or customs union and freedom of movement; Miliband affirmed these remain respected for this parliament while acknowledging that circumstances have changed materially since the 2016 vote. European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen expressed confidence a solution to the student-fee disagreement would be found.
items.title: UK Trade Agreements with EU Announced; Rejoining Bloc Kept as Open Option

items.summary: Despite gasoline prices falling nearly 60 cents in the past month, Americans traveling for Thanksgiving may still face higher pump costs than during any previous holiday. The national average dropped to $3.69 per gallon on Friday according to AAA, down from roughly $4.30 a year earlier, while GasBuddy projects an average of $3.62 on Thanksgiving Day—surpassing the prior record of $3.56 set in 2022. The decline reflects retreating crude oil prices and recovering supplies after disruptions tied to conflict involving Iran; West Texas Intermediate crude fell into the low $80s this week, U.S. gasoline inventories rose 5.1 million barrels to 215.9 million barrels, refineries switched to cheaper winter-blend fuel, and post-summer demand has softened. Travelers still pay about 60 cents more per gallon than last November, adding roughly $12 to a 500-mile round trip in a vehicle averaging 25 miles per gallon; AAA expects 72.9 million Americans to drive over the holiday versus 73.1 million the prior year, and GasBuddy reports nearly one in five drivers plans to cut other spending to cover fuel costs. Air travel offers little relief: AAA projects about 6 million flyers with domestic round-trip tickets averaging $800, up 17% from last Thanksgiving due to elevated jet fuel prices, while diesel averages around $5.90 per gallon and has pushed Thanksgiving dinner prices up 6%, according to the American Farm Bureau Federation. The outlook remains uncertain because Middle Eastern tanker traffic still faces attacks even as crude exports recover.
items.title: U.S. Gas Prices Could Hit a Thanksgiving Record Despite Month-Long Decline

items.summary: Rather than requiring separate apps, an expanding set of AI agents can be operated by texting them like ordinary people. These assistants reportedly remember context, connect to a user's existing email and calendar services, and complete tasks such as scheduling appointments, researching trips, sending emails, making reservations, shopping online, or setting reminders for later dates.
items.title: A growing roster of AI text-message agents competes for the personal-assistant space

items.summary: The 16th Biennale of Contemporary African Art opened in Dakar, Senegal, on Thursday under the theme "(Anti)fragility," which explores repair, resilience, and rebound as a way of transforming vulnerability into creative strength. The Democratic Republic of Congo is featured this year with its exhibition "Fourth Movement: Time as Living Matter." Curator Steve Bandoma describes the fourth movement as intangible, framing it as an encounter in front of a large mirror that prompts viewers to confront what has been done to people and Africa, examining the weight of history and each person's role. Ghanaian data artist Whitney Chinonye Ernest, part of a collective of women artists documenting the continent's journey toward democracy, says her participation lets her work reach hundreds or thousands of people and educate them about the effort behind African nations' milestones. Visitor Kuadio Adai noted it was his first time at the Biennale and described seeing the artwork as rewarding and powerful. Dak'Art 2026's official selection includes 54 artists from 17 African countries, with 22 in the Design section and three given carte blanche; around 450 projects are showcased across Dakar and other Senegalese cities until December 19.
items.title: Senegal's Dak'Art Biennale Opens Under Theme of (Anti)fragility

items.summary:
Shortical, a microdrama startup founded in January that produces short-form romantic series monetized primarily through subscriptions (typically the first 7–10 episodes are free before users pay to unlock full access), has begun pivoting toward AI-generated content because production costs for such material are substantially lower than live-action while profit potential is higher if an audience can be drawn. The company's latest microdrama, "Inevitable," premiered in Los Angeles and stars Aki Avni, a veteran Israeli actor with prior American television appearances including Fox's "24"; the project used his likeness to create a digital avatar playing himself in a meta plot about licensing one's face to a studio. This marked Shortical's first foray into likeness licensing, though CEO Guy Shimoni indicated it would likely not be its last.

In interviews with TechCrunch, Avni described the experience as both nerve-racking and exciting, framing AI as "a new kind of art" and himself as a pioneer in the format. Shimoni emphasized that AI enables smaller teams to produce movie-scale content—kingdoms, dragons, superheroes—that live-action budgets previously constrained. The company reported that while China has the largest microdrama audience globally, most of Shortical's viewers are U.S.-based; its demographic skews heavily female, with many watching at night for minor dopamine hits as they fall asleep, and several AI-generated titles reportedly have millions of views.

Shortical is now advertising a "LICENSE YOUR FACE" program on which interested parties submit social media handles to receive an offer setting out contract terms. A company representative stated this offering was still in its early days with no signed contracts yet, that the Avni series used a direct agreement rather than the platform process, and that Shortical hoped it would draw attention to face licensing before promoting the program more actively.

The trend has already taken hold in China, where microdrama originated. A Rest of World report found firms paying likenesses between US$15 and US$700, though one source noted this may not be particularly profitable for creators. Shortical declined to share Avni's specific figure but said his compensation was "in line with industry standards for a comparable non-AI acting role," while Shimoni answered vaguely whether royalty-based models like television residuals would apply—"a case by case [basis]."

Critics, including Jennifer Cooper of the consultancy Vertical Drama Love, expressed distrust of AI from both audiences and within the industry. She argued that automation has decimated a sector that previously provided entry-level work for young actors as companies downsize and produce content requiring no real performers. Consent concerns over stolen likenesses also persist; Shortical's licensing model is positioned partly to address these issues.

Cooper suggested AI adoption may be driven more by venture capital incentives than genuine demand, noting that investors expect startups to mention "AI"—which she compared to gold—and observing that much content gets little viewership. She characterized the trend as being pushed onto an audience rather than reflecting actual consumer desire.
items.title: Microdrama Startup Shortical Launches Paid Face-Licensing Program After Israeli Actor Aki Avni Becomes Its First AI Likeness Partner

items.summary: In an interview with Scroll, political theorist Manash Firaq Bhatcharjee discusses his book Gandhi: The End of Non-Violence, which examines Mahatma Gandhi's peace mission in Noakhali and Bihar during 1946-47 amid communal violence preceding India's Partition. Bhattacharjee argues that this period represents the least-known yet most heroic chapter of Gandhi's life—summarized by Marxist historian Sumit Sarkar as 'the Mahatma's finest hour'—yet it has never been exclusively studied or taught in Bengal, which he attributes to academic neglect and censorship by political regimes. He contends that Gandhi operated outside state frameworks during this period, refusing police assistance and instead pursuing interpersonal ethics of justice through prayer meetings, listening to victim accounts, singing Rabindrasangeet, and demanding confessions from perpetrators via private tribunals rather than legal processes. Bhattacharjee asserts that when the interim governments in Bengal and Bihar orchestrated Partition violence—evidenced by chief minister Huseyn Suhrawardy denying knowledge of historian Jadunath Sarkar's son's murder while Gandhi declared him responsible for every death—he recognized institutional justice was impossible, prompting Gandhi to rely on social morality. He frames Gandhi as acknowledging his own failure before Partition, viewing it within an epic historical encounter between Indian nationalism and British colonialism rather than blaming others. Critically, Bhattacharjee disputes existing historiography, arguing that scholars like Joya Chatterji (who blamed nationalist politics alone), Partha Chatterjee (attributing violence to 'elite politics'), and Janam Mukherjee (linking it to the 1943 Bengal famine) offered ideologically motivated causal explanations while neglecting moral dimensions. He maintains that Partition warrants philosophical rumination akin to how Jewish writers like Primo Levi, Hannah Arendt, and Paul Celan addressed the Holocaust—rather than reducing deaths to sociological details—and criticizes Jinnah for destroying 'the idea of the minority' by transforming it into a majoritarian movement while avoiding riot-torn areas. The interview presents these as Bhattacharjee's interpretations rather than established historical consensus.
items.title: Political theorist Manash Firaq Bhattacharjee argues historians have failed to capture the moral horror of Partition

items.summary: Ankur Choudhary, co-founder of Belong, a GIFT City-based savings and investment platform for non-resident Indians (NRIs), says the firm crossed $20 million in assets under management within about a year of its August 2025 launch, with investors from more than 20 countries. While USD fixed deposits and FCNR deposits still account for roughly three-quarters of AUM, Choudhary notes growing interest in GIFT City mutual funds and global products such as US stocks and ETFs. He attributes the shift to higher deposit rates (USD FDs up to 6%, with leveraged FCNR(B) deposits reaching 6-7% after RBI's June 2026 special window), Middle East conflict-driven safety-seeking flows, currency diversification benefits, and tax efficiency under the IFSC framework. Supporting data cited include active NRI demat accounts tripling from about 3.15 lakh in FY19 to over 9.5 lakh by July 2026 (with equity holdings rising from roughly ₹1.5 lakh crore to ₹5.6 lakh crore), GIFT City bank NRI accounts growing from about 3,700 in March 2024 to around 20,000-30,000 by mid-2026 (with deposits rising from $600 million to $1.96 billion per IFSCA), and GIFT City retail fund investors increasing from 255 in September 2025 to 8,467 in June 2026. Choudhary highlights regulatory tailwinds such as the raised NRI/OCI ownership limits (from 5% to 10%, combined up to 24%), remote KYC for FATF-compliant countries from December 3, 2026, and IFSCA's digital onboarding. He identifies potential future growth drivers including US options, foreign ETF listings, and commodity trading, while noting that fintechs still lag banks in core banking activities due to trust, regulatory backing, and physical presence. The interview is an edited excerpt from ETMarkets; figures are attributed to Choudhary or IFSCA/SEBI/RBI as stated.
items.title: Belong Crosses $20 Million AUM as NRIs Shift Toward GIFT City Mutual Funds and Global Investing

items.summary: Prime Minister Narendra Modi credited his appeal to citizens to limit gold purchases over the past year for contributing to a decline in gold prices, drawing a parallel with former Prime Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri's call for people to skip one meal during a food shortage. Speaking at the Kaushal Deekshant Samaroh in Lucknow on Saturday, Modi said ordinary citizens responded by buying less gold and reported that they were saving money as a result. He also highlighted Uttar Pradesh's growing role in semiconductor manufacturing—citing a chip factory being built there—and defence production, noting that BrahMos missiles used during Operation Sindoor are now manufactured in the state. On LPG availability amid concerns over the Strait of Hormuz crisis, Modi said the government decided to provide at least one lakh (100,000) PNG connections daily; he recounted a request for more than 15,000–20,000 that was answered with reports of a shortage of plumbers. He dismissed predictions of severe LPG shortages during the West Asia conflict as unfulfilled and said no one can take away the job of a skilled individual amid AI concerns. Modi called lifting 50 crore (500 million) people out of poverty since independence his country's greatest achievement, and announced that India will host the WorldSkills Asia competition in Greater Noida, Uttar Pradesh, in 2027.
items.title: Modi Credits Gold Purchase Appeal for Price Decline; Highlights UP Manufacturing and LPG Shortage Response

items.summary:
The FBI is reportedly investigating a second breach of its systems within two months, this time targeting the National Crime Information Center (NCIC), an FBI-operated database used by local, state, and federal law enforcement agencies for traffic stops, investigations, background checks, and records on wanted or missing persons, outstanding warrants, stolen vehicles and firearms, and protection orders. According to CNN's reporting—which cites two people briefed on the investigation—the intrusion was discovered in recent days, though it remains unclear when the breach occurred, how attackers gained access, whether any data was exfiltrated, or whether law enforcement availability of NCIC was disrupted. The FBI has not publicly confirmed the incident and did not respond to CNN's request for comment; BleepingComputer also reported no response after contacting the agency Friday evening.

The report follows a breach two months earlier attributed by the ShinyHunters extortion group, which claimed to have exploited an unpatched Oracle PeopleSoft vulnerability in a third-party platform tied to FBIJobs.gov and asserted it stole sensitive information. That investigation led to arrests of suspected ShinyHunters members, including a Canadian cybersecurity executive reportedly linked to the attacks.

There is currently no indication that the NCIC incident connects to ShinyHunters or the earlier breach, per CNN's reporting. The story remains developing and subject to change as more information becomes available; all claims are attributed to unnamed sources rather than confirmed by the FBI.
items.title: FBI Investigates Second NCIC Breach in Two Months; Link to Prior ShinyHunters Attack Unclear

items.summary: On November 21, Bitcoin rose more than 8 percent to around $59,952 on Saturday, briefly crossing the $60,000 mark at approximately 8:30 a.m. EST (1330 GMT), after sliding earlier that day to its lowest level in two years. The cryptocurrency had fallen to $55,251.60 before bouncing back. The decline was triggered by stretched valuations in artificial intelligence stocks and broader risk-off sentiment; Bitcoin broke below $57,742 for the first time since September 2024 as AI-infrastructure profitability concerns weighed on investors. Contributing headwinds included a stronger dollar, higher real yields, greater market volatility, regulatory uncertainty following Democrats' win in the US midterm elections, and the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The rebound occurred against a backdrop of continued weakness in equities: US stocks extended their rout Friday into one of their steepest weekly declines since April 2025 (the 'Liberation Day' tariffs), with S&P 500 and Dow corrections amplified by a disappointing debut for Anthropic, which further rattled the AI trade. The article notes that Bitcoin has increasingly moved in tandem with stocks amid these conditions.
items.title: Bitcoin rebounds above $59,000 after two-year low

items.summary: San Diego-based Unigrid, whose development team grew out of University of California, San Diego research, is pursuing sodium-ion battery chemistries to serve market segments it says are poorly suited to lithium-ion. CEO Darren Tan told pv magazine USA that sodium-ion offers better safety (non-flammable), long cycle and calendar life, and wide thermal tolerance across a stated discharge range of about -100°F to +140°F with charging down to about -68°F; the main tradeoff is greater weight and space. Its 48V Na+ Casa series targets commercial and residential storage and is UN38.3 certified and tested to UL 9540A at the cell level, which Tan says makes it suitable for indoor deployment such as hospitals or multi-unit housing. Unigrid frames lithium-ion's dominance of midrange two- to six-hour endurance needs partly on its bankability and financing access, while identifying short-duration storage—minutes to seconds between supercapacitors and batteries—as an emerging gap driven by AI-driven grid strains shifting demand toward ancillary services like demand response, uninterruptible loads, and load-shifting-based demand charges. Tan notes lithium-ion is poorly suited to high-power quick responses and frequent cycling (e.g., 10-20 cycles per day in data-center contexts), that the prevailing alternative has been lithium-titanate oxide batteries at roughly 20 times the cost of lithium-ion, and that sodium-ion offers high power, long cycle life, wide temperature ranges without cooling, safety, and price competitiveness. Tan says Unigrid's main challenges are achieving third-party testing benchmarks and regulatory certification for U.S. deployment—hurdles he notes lithium-ion suppliers have largely cleared—and plans to lean on European and other international installations while hoping rising fuel prices will attract developers and financiers.
items.title: Unigrid positions sodium-ion batteries for short-duration storage gaps where lithium-ion underperforms

items.summary: Prime Minister Balendra Shah of Nepal is scheduled to arrive in India on Sunday for a two-day state visit, marking his first trip since assuming office in March. During the visit he will hold talks with Prime Minister Narendra Modi and also call on President Droupadi Murmu and meet External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar. According to Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal, the discussions will cover development cooperation, people-to-people ties, energy ties, connectivity, and emerging areas such as startups, technology, innovation, sports, and cricket links. Shah is also expected to seek India's assistance in rebuilding infrastructure damaged by August floods that reportedly claimed 1,500 lives, left over 5,200 missing, and destroyed roads, bridges, power facilities, agricultural land, and homes. Another agenda item involves Nepal's demand for an additional air route connecting western Nepal to Bhairahawa near Lumbini and Pokhara. Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle and business representatives will accompany Shah on the trip.
items.title: Nepal's PM Balendra Shah to meet India's PM Modi during state visit

items.summary: El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele deployed approximately 2,000 Salvadoran soldiers to Haiti—largely to rescue four compatriots from a U.N.-led mission—but the contingent has become his broader attempt to replicate what he calls the 'Bukele model' of pacification. The deployment is the largest since the United Nations Stabilization Mission in Haiti (MINUSTAH), which operated there from 2004 to 2017, and includes special forces members. However, the agreement between Bukele and Haitian Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé remains undisclosed: its duration, objectives, oversight structure, and operational command have not been made public, with troops currently answering directly to Bukele—who has a well-documented record of human rights violations—rather than to local authorities. This lack of coordination stands out against the other four forces operating in Haiti: the Haitian National Police (PNH), the Haitian Armed Forces, the Task Force (linked to U.S. security firm Vectus Global), and the UN-led Gang Suppression Force (GSF). Romain Le Cour, director of the Haiti Observatory at Global Initiative for Transparency in Conflict (GI-TOC), described the situation as 'an orchestra without a conductor,' noting that unclear roles also obscure accountability if something goes wrong.
items.title: Salvadoran Troops Deployed in Haiti Amid Poor Coordination and Human Rights Concerns

items.summary: An analysis of the Australian 10-year-3-month term spread finds that inversions do not reliably predict recessions, even when tested against alternative recession chronologies. The study compares three definitions: ECRI-defined peak-to-trough dates (shaded light blue), Melbourne Institute-defined unemployment-based trough-to-peak dates (light green), and a modified Sahm rule using a 75 basis-point threshold instead of the standard 50 bps, with end dates assumed equal to ECRI's. While ECRI and the Melbourne Institute largely agree on mid-1980s and 1990-91 recessions and both called off a 2009 recession, they disagree on the 1970s recessions; notably, the modified Sahm rule would have flagged recessions in 2001 and 2009 that did not feature sustained declines in total employment or GDP. Predictive performance is weak: over the full sample of 1986-26 months, no recession was predicted with a pseudo-R-squared greater than 0.14, and the spread's coefficient carried the opposite sign to what would be expected. Restricting the sample to the pre-pandemic period raised the pseudo-R-squared to as high as 50% for either chronology, but the spread still retained its incorrect sign. The author notes that this lack of predictive power for recessions is distinct from the term spread's documented ability to predict GDP growth (citing Poke and Wells, 2009). Unemployment rate data are available only from February 1978 onward, so no Sahm rule-based recession dates exist before February 1979. A limitation of this analysis is that it does not provide a chart comparing the term spread against each chronology.
items.title: Term Spread Inversions Do Not Predict Australian Recessions

items.summary: Thinking Machines Lab released Inkling 2 Mini, an open-weight looped Mixture-of-Experts model with 26.4B total parameters (3.4B active), designed to run locally on a 32GB Mac or one NVIDIA DGX Spark. The architecture stores 24 layers in four blocks of six—the first and last running once while the two middle blocks each repeat three times using shared weights—yielding 48 layer applications per token from only 24 stored layers, with feed-forward routing through 128 experts (8 active per token). Thinking Machines reports this looping produced a 1.51x to 1.91x compute-equivalent gain on the middle layers versus 1.24x to 1.36x for last-layer looping, and that an unlooped baseline required 140% more inference compute to match the looped model's loss; however, these efficiency figures are self-reported by the vendor. The checkpoint is approximately 20GB in Safetensors format under Apache 2.0, supports up to a 1M-token context, and accepts text plus images while returning text only. On coding benchmarks—self-reported—the model scores 79.2% on SWE-bench Verified (bash only), 77.9% on SWE-bench Pro v2 (Hard), and 48.2% on DeepSWE v1.1, where it edges out Qwen3.8-27B's reported 42.2%, though it trails that model at 71.6% versus 73.0% on Terminal Bench v2.1; Thinking Machines also claims a self-reported Artificial Analysis Index score of 20.1, tied with Qwen3.8-27B. The vendor lists efficiency as its headline claim, reporting an Intelligence per Watt metric of 0.703 on a DGX Spark versus 0.430 for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and 0.159 for Gemma-4-26B-A4B, though these cross-vendor comparisons rely on differing model cards and harnesses. Inkling 2 Mini follows the larger 594B-parameter Inkling 2 Small released November 5. The primary limitation is that looping did not improve knowledge benchmarks: the model scores -8.6 on AA-Omniscience with a reported 63.4% non-hallucination rate, and it underperforms on multi-turn chat (50.0% on MultiChallenge) and constraint-heavy prompts (33.4% on ComplexConstraints v1.1), while also trailing larger models at 15.2% on HLE-Diamond.
items.title: Thinking Machines Releases Inkling 2 Mini: A Looped MoE Model Running on Consumer Hardware

items.summary: The Solar Energy Corporation of India (SECI) cancelled its tender to lease two parcels of agricultural land in the National Capital Territory (NCT) of Delhi for developing agri-photovoltaic (Agri-PV) power plants. The cancellation was announced through an official tender annulment notice, ending the bidding process under Tender No. SECI/C&P/MI/00/05/2026-27, originally issued on September 9, 2026. Agri-PV projects combine agricultural cultivation with solar power generation on the same land, allowing farmers to continue farming while generating electricity and expanding renewable energy capacity without fully replacing agriculture. The annulment notice provided no specific reason for the cancellation, and SECI did not indicate whether it would issue a fresh tender or pursue another procurement process for Agri-PV development in Delhi. Interested parties were directed to monitor SECI's official website for further announcements regarding agricultural land leasing.
items.title: SECI Cancels Tender for Two Delhi Agricultural Land Agri-PV Projects

items.summary: Despite raising the most cash ever from an initial public offering and pricing above its target range, Anthropic PBC's stock plateaued after launching and fell about $6 by Friday's close, failing to lift sentiment in an AI trade that continued selling off. The Nasdaq 100 Index dropped 10% for the week—its worst performance since March 2020—as chipmakers led declines amid a looming Federal Reserve interest-rate hike and broader skepticism over whether technology is adapting to AI risks. Anthropic's underwhelming debut reinforced doubts about meeting lofty near-term expectations, according to Jim Baird of Plante Moran Financial Advisors. Structural concerns compound the weakness: Democratic midterm gains raise fears that data center construction will slow as many candidates ran on blocking it, while higher rates increase capital costs for developers relying on credit markets—factors Malcolm Polley of Stratos Investment Management says constrain how AI-driven assets can be valued. Nvidia's turmoil added to investor unease after it ousted CEO Jensen Huang on Nov. 12 over an affair with a woman suspected of spying for China; despite strong earnings and a $150 billion buyback authorization, shares plunged 23% in the week (worst since 2008) and fell 48% from their Oct. 6 all-time high. Competitor Advanced Micro Devices also tumbled about 20% after short-seller questions raised concerns over its China business amid potential export restrictions. The selloff reflects skepticism toward hundreds of billions in computing-power spending that had driven the Philadelphia Stock Exchange Semiconductor Index to more than double in the first half of the year before losing 41% in the second half as cyclical fears resurfaced. Strategists remain divided: Brian Smedley of Cynosure Strategies expects the oversold market to stabilize and AI demand to stay strong, while Mark Luschini of Janney Montgomery Scott cautions that investors still lack clarity on what could catalyze gains and warns the selloff could deepen before stabilizing.
items.title: Wall Street Searches for a Catalyst After Anthropic IPO Fails to Rescue AI Trade

items.summary: Anthropic's stock fell about 9% from its Thursday debut close to $88.87, leaving a fully diluted valuation of roughly $1.6 trillion and a market capitalization of around $1.2 trillion based on shares outstanding. The decline raised questions about whether the company can sustain a valuation near 40 times sales over the past 12 months, which analysts say assumes years of rapid growth. Kaush Amin, head of private market investing at US Bank Asset Management, advised patience and evaluating Anthropic as it reports public results. Near-term volatility may persist as initial enthusiasm fades; options trading due to begin next week could add pressure, though London-based Intropic estimates index-tracking funds could buy up to 30% of shares by year-end, potentially supporting the stock later in the year.
items.title: Anthropic's Post-IPO Decline Signals Cooling for the AI Trade

items.summary: Elon Musk, chief of Tesla and xAI, warned that the global artificial intelligence industry could face a severe cash shortage in 2027 because companies must pay for hardware months before it can reliably generate revenue. The warning came in response to AI researcher François Chollet, who noted intense demand reflected in rising GPU spot prices and sold-out high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and DRAM production. Musk argued that physical execution—purchasing chips, building data centers, securing power supplies, and installing cooling systems—is the immediate financial threat rather than market appetite. He wrote on X that even cumulative industry delays of a few months between paying for compute and getting it reliable enough to earn revenue would require hundreds of billions of dollars in incremental working capital, questioning where such funds would come from. Supporting figures cited by Goldman Sachs (via Crypto Briefing) show 2026 AI capital expenditures nearing $1 trillion, backed by nearly $600 billion in global AI-related debt issuance. Musk acknowledged that inference can deliver 70-85% margins once operational, but the upfront cash burn to bridge construction and grid-connection delays is escalating. Analysts note tighter credit conditions could hit specialized 'neocloud' providers hardest because they rely on debt markets for GPU financing and cannot absorb multi-month deployment lags like cash-rich tech conglomerates can; Musk has repeatedly flagged electricity and thermal management as the primary constraints, previously estimating a global AI chip power shortfall of at least 15 gigawatts by 2027. The figures are drawn from Goldman Sachs data cited through Crypto Briefing, while Musk's deployment-timing estimate is his own projection without an attached source.
items.title: Elon Musk Warns AI Industry Faces Cash Crunch in 2027 Over Compute Deployment Delays

items.summary: NASA announced that its Voyager 1 spacecraft reached a distance of one light-day—about 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers)—from Earth at 2:16 a.m. PST on Nov. 18, roughly 49 years after the probe launched Sept. 5, 1977. At this range, radio signals travel at light speed and take about 24 hours to reach the spacecraft and another 24 hours to return; NASA confirmed the milestone using a carrier signal rather than science data, which had not been received since Nov. 14 because of an ongoing technical issue that engineers are still analyzing. The mission is managed by JPL for Caltech, with Voyager 1 having become humanity's first spacecraft to cross into interstellar space in Dec. 2012 and its twin Voyager 2 following in 2018; both probes continue measuring the Sun's magnetic field while conserving power from their aging radioisotope thermal generators, which lose about 4 watts per year as plutonium depletes. Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman commented on X that reaching one light-day is incredible and noted the spacecraft was built with 1970s technology; NASA officials Joe Westlake, Dave Gallagher, Linda Spilker, Suzanne Dodd, and Caltech president Ray Jayawardhana also weighed in on the mission's scientific contributions and engineering challenges. The article contains no stated forecast or explicit limitation beyond noting that science data transmission remains unresolved.
items.title: NASA's Voyager 1 Reaches One Light-Day from Earth After Nearly 49 Years of Travel

items.summary:
At the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen, economies adopted a statement titled 'Harnessing Digital and Emerging Technologies for Employment and Prosperity in the Asia-Pacific Region,' which links industrial upgrading with workforce development and worker protection. The document calls for using digital technologies to drive innovation, improve productivity, and support high-quality full employment across sectors including energy, agriculture, education, transportation, healthcare, and micro-, small- and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs). It also emphasizes helping workers adapt through improved digital access and literacy, expanded vocational training, better-matched job-seeking services, and protections for worker rights, working conditions, and occupational safety. The APEC Human Resource Development Working Group is designated to coordinate implementation with other relevant bodies.

Experts offered interpretations rather than official endorsements: Jiang Tianjiao of Fudan University's Development Institute suggested APEC could help bridge the AI divide through open technologies, shared application scenarios, and joint risk management; Alejandro Reyes of the University of Hong Kong stressed that technology access alone is insufficient without effective use, cooperation on computing resources, language-specific models, and worker training—particularly in developing economies. The text notes these are expert perspectives rather than adopted positions.

The article contains no stated limitations or caveats beyond attributing analytical claims to their respective experts.
items.title: APEC Adopts Statement on Harnessing Digital Technologies for Employment in Asia-Pacific

items.summary: Song Xiangcai, a 33-year-old former product manager from Jinan who relocated to Shanghai in 2017 and was laid off during a company restructuring, began volunteering at airports after seeing others do so online. He performs the work without pay, covering his own round-trip fares and food costs initially through savings before generating income via social media traffic, advertising revenue, and small commercial sponsorships—though he still earns considerably less than as a product manager. His family was initially unsupportive due to concerns about finances after his marriage last year but came around once the content grew popular enough to cover part of their living costs. Song began documenting his volunteer work on social media in November of last year, and his videos depict him assisting visitors with directions, helping lost-phone travelers, or simply greeting them while learning languages such as Russian, Japanese, Korean, and Spanish—though he notes these are limited to practical phrases sufficient for basic needs like giving directions. He has taught Chinese to some visitors and shared footage of their attempts, but acknowledges that not every encounter is pleasant despite the overall positive response. Song attributes his motivation partly to mood-boosting dopamine and endorphins released when helping others, a factor he describes as nearly addictive. His stated goals include offering viewers an authentic window into everyday life in China to counter biased portrayals of the country rather than staging encounters, while also hoping Chinese audiences learn about other cultures; he plans to continue learning languages and improving his English.
items.title: Chinese Airport Volunteer Gains Online Following After Documenting Cross-Cultural Encounters

items.summary: The Chamber of Trade and Industry (CTI) wrote to Prime Minister Narendra Modi thanking him for his appeal urging citizens to avoid unnecessary gold purchases, stating the advice helped protect jewellers, traders, and investors from losses after a decline in gold prices. In a letter dated Sunday titled 'Your foresight saved lakhs of jewellers and investors from falling into debt,' CTI said the appeal had drawn criticism when first made but ultimately aided traders. According to the trade body, gold was priced at Rs 1.90 crore per kilogram when Modi issued his advice; it has since fallen to Rs 1.25 crore per kilogram, a decline of Rs 65 lakh per kilogram. CTI stated that had traders bought inventory at the earlier price, they would have incurred losses worth crores today, as jewellery traders typically maintain several months' stock and are exposed to significant downside risk. The organisation also noted that small online and offline gold dealers and stock market investors were similarly protected, with messages pouring into its groups thanking Modi for his advice. CTI added the price fall offered relief during a wedding season it said was witnessing 52 lakh weddings. The letter was signed by CTI chairman Brijesh Goyal and other office-bearers.
items.title: CTI Credits Modi's Gold Purchase Appeal for Averting Trader Losses

items.summary: Rising domestic airfares in India are preventing working migrants from traveling home for major life events during festival and wedding seasons. The increases stem largely from airlines citing higher fuel costs linked to the Iran war, making short-notice trips unaffordable—especially since trains are unavailable on demand. Clinical psychology student Aditi abandoned plans to fly from Delhi to Kolkata for 'bhai phota' after a Rs 23,000 round-trip fare; media professional Ananya Nair will watch her best friend's Dec 6 Kerala wedding online rather than pay an upward of Rs 30,000 round trip (cheapest direct morning flight from Delhi to Kochi at Rs 17,000 one-way); and first-time aunt Kavya missed her niece's July naming ceremony after a cheapest one-way fare of Rs 11,800. Salon professional Riya Sharma said the Jabalpur round trip exceeded 50% of her monthly income (cheapest flight at Rs 8,000 via Hyderabad), and Vasant could not attend his uncle's death in Bhubaneswar because fares approached Rs 27,000 for a round trip. A Times of India check on Nov 21 found one-way Delhi fares near Rs 20,000 at Christmas (Dec 25) and New Year's Day (Jan 1), with the highest prices in the Delhi-Bengaluru, Delhi-Kolkata, and Delhi-Ahmedabad sectors. Reduced seat availability—partly due to Air India cutting services on several routes—further pushed fares up; a Bengaluru-to-Patna one-way reportedly cost Rs 25,000 during Chhath Puja, prompting some travelers to use tempos with trains fully booked. The Supreme Court declined an urgent Nov 2 plea for a fare cap, noting petitioner claims of surges as high as 700% on some routes; Justice Vikram Nath dismissed the argument that air travel is essential by telling counsel 'Don't travel by air.' Findings are based on individual accounts and limited TOI fare checks rather than comprehensive data.
items.title: Sky-high Indian airfares force migrant families to miss weddings, births, and funerals

items.summary: A fire at a confectionery factory in Serang district, Banten province—about 50km west of Jakarta—killed at least three people and left 36 still missing as of Sunday. Firefighters were still battling flames on the site while rescuers searched for workers believed to be trapped inside the damaged building. Indonesia's National Search and Rescue Agency reported that 15 survivors had been located, with four others taken to a hospital and local clinic with undisclosed injuries. Banten Governor Andra Soni said roughly 60 people were believed to have been inside the factory when it caught fire during the night. Firefighters were called at 1630 local time (0930 GMT), but the building was already engulfed in flames, so officials could not determine whether the company's protection system had functioned properly; the cause of the fire remains undetermined. The facility is owned by PT Fonusa Agung Mulia, a subsidiary of UNIFAM, one of Indonesia's largest food and beverage companies.
items.title: Fire at confectionery factory in western Java leaves dozens missing

On 11 November, the Kraftwerk Berlin arts complex converted its central hall into a militarised space to launch Clarity, an agentic intelligence targeting system developed by Munich-based arms startup Helsing. The venue displayed war-room imagery including maps and aerial footage on concrete walls, hung drones overhead, and deployed guards in flak jackets with sniffer dogs for the event. Visitors described the atmosphere as dystopian even for Berlin's techno scene, prompting Kraftwerk to apologise for a 'serious error of judgment' and vow to revise its commercial rental booking policy after outrage spread through the city's music community.

Helsing was founded in 2021 with Spotify co-founder Daniel Ek among its investors. The company describes Clarity as using drone, satellite and sensor data to lock on to targets while human operators approve strikes, claiming it is developed under European control. A Helsing spokesperson told broadcaster RBB that none of its systems were designed to identify persons but instead target objects such as radar systems, launch pads and ships, though the company's agents also specialise in 'looking for patterns of behaviour' that could relate to human activity.

The event drew sharp condemnation from Tresor nightclub and record label, whose founder Dimitri Hegemann—who is also Kraftwerk Berlin's managing director—called the booking unacceptable because it was arranged by a commercial rental staff member without his consultation. Music curator Michail Stangl argued that Germany supporting Ukraine should not mean abandoning critical faculties about AI targeting systems already used in Gaza.

The controversy highlights tensions between European governments seeking alternatives to US battlefield software like Palantir's Maven and Berlin's anti-militaristic cultural heritage, where nightclubs historically served as spaces to escape arms-race anxieties. Kraftwerk noted it had declined a 2022 Palantir-sponsored event after consulting its cultural teams.

Defenders point out that many Berlin clubs struggle with rising rents and falling bar revenues, though Schaltraum Berlin—the operating company behind Kraftwerk—reported total assets of €4.3m (£3.6m) in June as potentially more financially secure.
items.title: Kraftwerk Berlin Apologises After Hosting Helsing's Military AI Targeting System at Nightclub Venue

items.summary: More than 20 Labour MPs have signed up for a year-long leadership programme designed to help them counter rightwing populism and manage hostility, according to reporting on the scheme. The training is worth about £9,600 per course and is led by Ruth Turner—former director of government relations at No 10—and Peter Hyman, who has worked across Blair, Keir Starmer, and Andy Burnham's governments. About 18 MPs, including former ministers Dawn Butler, Rachel Blake, and Fleur Anderson, confirmed attendance at a three-day residential course run by August Ltd, the company owned by Turner; several additional MPs have been trained without attending the awaydays. The programme is ultimately funded by grant from Gary Lubner, who made his fortune running Autoglass and has donated more than £11m to Labour and the thinktank formerly known as Labour Together (now ThinkLabour). Under the terms of that grant, Lubner does not have any influence over or input into the course. The sessions focus on three themes—resilience, agency, and teamwork—and cover countering far-right populism, including how algorithms can radicalise people and exploit their grievances. Turner said she and Hyman developed the idea after observing MPs being thrust into Parliament without adequate preparation; from her No 10 experience she noted that senior officials making consequential decisions were often kept isolated and unsupported, while backbenchers remained undertrained compared with ministers who receive training from bodies such as the Institute for Government. She described the programme's emphasis on individual resilience in light of the physical threat and hostility MPs face, teamwork to counter a hyper-individualised and competitive sector, and an aim to normalise training across Parliament. The reporting notes that entering Commons members do not receive mandatory job or leadership training, are not employed by the House of Commons, and operate effectively as self-employed individuals responsible for their own development.
items.title: Over 20 Labour MPs Enrol in Leadership Course to Counter Rightwing Populism

items.summary: Countries preparing to resume negotiations at the UN COP31 summit in Antalya faced a possible collapse as a new draft agreement was published in the early hours of Sunday. The text, co-hosted by Turkey and Australia with Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum presiding over the talks, aimed to bridge divisions but still contains no specific reference to transitioning away from fossil fuels—an omission that had sparked walkout threats after an earlier pared-down version stripped out all mentions of coal, oil and gas. The draft does acknowledge a prior commitment made three years ago regarding such transition and includes for the first time at a COP a recognition that the world is on track to miss its Paris Agreement goal of keeping warming below 1.5C, entering what scientists call an "overshoot" period with warnings of expanded sea level rise and extreme heat exposure.
items.title: New draft climate deal published hours before UN COP31 talks risk suspension

According to an interview with PTI published on November 22, 2026, Mahindra Last Mile Mobility Ltd (MLMML) is considering a public listing in approximately 18 months. The company's Chairman Rajesh Jejurikar stated that the timeline remains broad and unconfirmed because MLMML has not finalized a listing date; he emphasized that management wished to avoid distraction from the IPO process. As of the interview, MLMML held an estimated valuation of around $1 billion with two investors on board and a third expected soon. Jejurikar noted that proceeds would be used partly for value unlocking but primarily to fund growth in new segments and products as well as capacity expansion, while Mahindra intends to retain its stake rather than significantly reduce it.

On product strategy, MLMML is targeting electric three- and four-wheelers across both passenger and cargo categories. Jejurikar clarified that the company would maintain its focus on last-mile urban transportation instead of intercity mobility, though he declined to specify particular products. Regarding demand trends, he observed that passenger electric three-wheelers had driven growth so far while cargo vehicles were expected to gain momentum.

For overseas expansion, MLMML is exploring Southeast Asia, Africa, and possibly Western markets, with Earthshot Prize recognition anticipated to facilitate global partnerships; however, Jejurikar cautioned that international entry would require time for assessing product suitability, business potential, EV penetration levels, and the development of distribution, spare-parts, and service ecosystems. He added that although the company received enquiries following the award, it had not yet conducted detailed work on its global strategy.

The text also notes a distinction between two awards: MLMML will use one million pounds from the Earthshot Prize to support women aspiring to become drivers rather than for business expansion. On pricing and incentives, Jejurikar explained that FAME and PM E-DRIVE subsidies were no longer available for this category, leaving only the production-linked incentive (PLI) scheme; he attributed future pricing headroom to material cost optimization from higher volumes combined with customers recognizing EV economic benefits.

items.title: Mahindra Last Mile Mobility Chairman Signals IPO Within 18 Months Amid Product and Overseas Expansion Plans

items.summary: According to a Registrar of Companies filing published on November 22, 2026, Reliance Brands Ltd (RBL), a subsidiary of Reliance Retail Ventures Ltd that operates global fashion and lifestyle brands in India through partnerships, brand ownership, and retail operations, reported revenue from operations rising 3.77% to ₹3,390.89 crore for FY26, compared with ₹3,267.66 crore in FY25. The company narrowed its loss to approximately ₹137 crore (reported as ₹137.04 crore and ₹137.13 crore across the filing), down from a profit of ₹237.12 crore recorded in FY25, with last year's prior-year comparison figure cited at ₹233.79 crore loss. The company manages a portfolio spanning luxury, bridge-to-luxury, premium, and high-street fashion, plus F&B, eyewear, home & lifestyle, and toys, serving an estimated 12–15 million affluent Indian consumers. As of March 31, 2026, RBL operated 1,085 Points of Sale across India through proprietary concepts such as The Whitecrow, The Books & Café, and Tank, alongside over 90 partner brands. During FY26 the company added three global master franchise partnerships—Stella McCartney, MAX&Co, and Kurt Geiger—and entered athleisure with Fabletics; it also holds six subsidiaries, 11 joint ventures, four associate companies, and owns Hamleys, a toy retailer operating in 13 countries. The figures are drawn from the company's RoC filing and financial data accessed via Tofler, though some values differ slightly between sources within the report.
items.title: Reliance Brands Reports FY26 Revenue Growth and Narrowing Loss

items.summary: South Korea's education minister Choi Kyo-jin resigned on Sunday following an AI-assisted cheating scandal that intensified in the lead-up to the country's annual university entrance exam, the eight-hour suneung. The crisis began last Sunday when the top scorer of a national tax accountant exam admitted using a miniature camera and smartphone to achieve a near-perfect score just four days before the suneung, prompting officials to scramble for preventive measures such as blocking public wifi in testing areas. Despite these efforts, teachers' unions criticized the government's response as belated, and Choi struggled to reassure the public; during a parliamentary hearing he told reporters that due to his age (72) he was not confident authorities could catch would-be cheaters on exam day, drawing immediate backlash. He did not attend press conferences in the days before Thursday's exam, when a vice minister announced measures instead. The government had required smart devices to be turned off and handed in for the suneung, instructed officials to inspect candidates' glasses, watches, collars, sleeves and buttons for concealed cameras, checked bags left in corridors, and sent emergency alerts that sounded at full volume and could not be silenced. Officials reported 111 cases of misconduct involving electronic devices during Thursday's exam, nearly half detected through the emergency alerts. The article notes no independent verification of these figures or the effectiveness of the measures beyond official claims.
items.title: South Korea education minister resigns after AI cheating scandal engulfs suneung exams

items.summary: A new NBER paper models economic growth in developed and developing economies where AI services are traded globally, allowing for substitution or complementarity with labor inputs. The model predicts that developing countries may gain less from AI-driven growth because they could lack complementary skills to fully use AI domestically and risk being priced out of world markets due to lower productivity. Numerical simulations suggest the potential for these countries to be left behind—or for some workers to lose in absolute terms—is substantial enough to warrant studying AI's impacts on developing economies in real time.
items.title: NBER Paper Argues Developing Countries May Benefit Less From AI-Driven Growth

items.summary: A fire at the Fonusa Agung Mulia candy-making factory in Serang, Banten province—about 50 kilometers west of Jakarta—killed at least three people on Saturday afternoon while leaving 36 workers unaccounted for as rescue teams searched Sunday. The blaze began in a cooling unit on the third floor and destroyed large sections of the three-story building, bringing down its roof in places; drone footage captured the damage. Governor Andra Soni said roughly 60 people were believed to be inside when the fire broke out, while search-and-rescue official Rizky Dwianto reported that four injured workers had been taken to a nearby hospital and clinic and eleven others rescued alive. The factory produces Milkita, an Indonesian brand of milk-based candies and snacks. Officials noted Indonesia has experienced several recent deadly industrial fires: at least 22 people died in December when a fire broke out in a seven-story Jakarta building after a suspected drone battery explosion, and at least 13 were killed in a nickel-processing plant explosion elsewhere in the country in 2023.
items.title: Fire at Indonesian candy factory leaves dozens missing and kills at least three

items.summary: Paolo Bulgari, the grandson of Greek silversmith Sotirios Voulgaris and longtime head of the jewellery company he helped build into a global luxury brand, has died at age 89. His family announced his death on Saturday (Nov 21), describing him as 'the greatest jeweller of our time' while praising his humanity and entrepreneurial talent. Born in Rome in 1937, Bulgari joined the business shortly after leaving school to work alongside his father Giorgio, developing expertise in precious stones that shaped his later design and business career. Heading the group since the mid-1980s, he guided a period of significant international growth, opening stores in New York, Paris, Geneva and Monte Carlo with brothers Nicola Bulgari and nephew Francesco Trapani, and diversifying the company into watches, perfumes, leather goods and hotels. The brand's bold aesthetic—rich yellow gold, generous proportions, unexpected colour combinations and inspiration drawn from ancient Rome—distinguished it internationally, making its jewellery a fixture among celebrities ranging from Elizabeth Taylor to Zendaya. In 2011, the family sold a controlling stake in the company to French luxury conglomerate LVMH in a deal valued at more than US$5 billion, ending decades of direct family control. Beyond his commercial work, Bulgari established the Paolo Bulgari Foundation in 2019 with his wife to support young people through schooling and job training in disadvantaged neighbourhoods on Rome's outskirts; he wrote that 'at the origin of my surname there is a story of migration.' His funeral will be held Monday at the Basilica of Santa Croce in Rome.
items.title: Paolo Bulgari, Italian jeweller who led family brand into global luxury status, dies aged 89
